title: Upgrade-Safe Scripting Patterns in ServiceNow: From Script Includes to Safe Refactoring
excerpt: A practical guide to writing upgrade-safe scripts in ServiceNow, covering Script Includes, GlideRecord best practices, avoiding hard‑coded sys_ids, using system properties, and safely refactoring legacy logic. Includes three realistic code examples and a short anti‑pattern section for comparison.
content:
Overview

ServiceNow upgrades are frequent and opinionated: every release brings new platform behavior, security controls, and out-of-the-box (OOB) logic. To avoid painful merge conflicts and brittle apps, developers need upgrade-safe scripting patterns that minimize custom surface area, isolate change, and make future refactors predictable.

This article focuses on five practical areas: Script Includes, GlideRecord best practices, avoiding hard-coded sys_ids, using system properties, and safe refactoring of legacy code. Examples assume scoped apps but apply equally to global with minor adjustments.

Script Includes as the Backbone of Upgrade-Safe Logic

Script Includes should be your primary home for reusable server-side logic. They keep Business Rules, UI Actions, and Flow actions thin, making it easier to compare and reconcile when upgrades introduce changed behavior.

Key patterns for Script Includes

  • Single responsibility: Each Script Include should do one job (e.g., calculate SLA targets, encapsulate approval rules). This lowers the chance you must touch the same class in multiple upgrade cycles.
  • Public vs. private API methods: Expose a small set of stable methods (public API) and keep helpers private (via naming convention like _helper()). When you refactor internals, callers remain unaffected.
  • Scoped, non-client callable by default: Mark as client-callable only when absolutely necessary and create a narrow wrapper for that purpose. This limits unintended coupling and security exposure.
  • Version-tolerant signatures: When changing a public method signature, prefer optional parameter objects instead of long ordered argument lists. This allows you to add new options without breaking existing calls.

Code example 1: Upgrade-safe Script Include API

var TaskLifecycle = Class.create();
TaskLifecycle.prototype = {
    initialize: function() {},

    processTask: function(taskGr, options) {
        options = options || {};
        if (!taskGr || !taskGr.isValidRecord())
            throw 'TaskLifecycle: invalid GlideRecord';

        if (options.skipNotifications !== true)
            this._sendNotifications(taskGr);

        if (options.autoClose === true && this._isClosable(taskGr))
            this._closeTask(taskGr);
    },

    _sendNotifications: function(taskGr) {
        // internal logic; safe to refactor between upgrades
    },

    _isClosable: function(taskGr) {
        return taskGr.state == '3'; // example: Resolved
    },

    _closeTask: function(taskGr) {
        taskGr.state = '4';
        taskGr.update();
    },

    type: 'TaskLifecycle'
};

Callers only rely on processTask() and the options object. You can safely refactor helpers or add new options later with minimal upgrade impact.

GlideRecord Best Practices for Upgrade Safety

GlideRecord misuse is a common source of performance and data issues, which upgrades tend to expose. Robust, defensive queries are inherently more upgrade-safe because they behave predictably when schemas and data volumes change.

Core GlideRecord patterns

  • Never query with undefined/null: Always check parameters before adding encoded queries. An undefined field can pull back an entire table and cause timeouts or data corruption.
  • Limit row sets: Use setLimit() for utilities where you only need a sample or a bounded number of records.
  • Use indexed fields: Prefer queries on indexed columns (e.g., sys_id, number, foreign keys) to avoid full table scans that become brittle at scale.
  • Encapsulate queries: Wrap complex queries in Script Includes so future schema changes are localized.
  • Check isValidRecord(): After get(), always verify you have a valid record before using it.

Code example 2: Defensive GlideRecord usage

var IncidentUtils = Class.create();
IncidentUtils.prototype = {
    initialize: function() {},

    findByNumber: function(incNumber) {
        if (!incNumber)
            return null;

        var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
        gr.addQuery('number', incNumber);
        gr.setLimit(1);
        gr.query();
        if (gr.next())
            return gr;

        return null;
    },

    getOpenByCaller: function(callerId) {
        if (!callerId)
            return [];

        var results = [];
        var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
        gr.addQuery('caller_id', callerId);
        gr.addQuery('active', true);
        gr.orderByDesc('priority');
        gr.setLimit(50);
        gr.query();
        while (gr.next())
            results.push(gr.sys_id.toString());

        return results;
    },

    type: 'IncidentUtils'
};

This pattern avoids unbounded queries, validates inputs, and keeps query rules centralized. If the incident table gains new constraints or indexes in a future release, you only adjust this Script Include.

Avoiding Hard-Coded sys_ids and Magic Values

Hard-coded sys_ids and magic constants are a top cause of brittle customizations. They break when records are deleted, re-seeded, or differ between instances, and they complicate clone and upgrade work.

Safer alternatives to hard-coded sys_ids

  • System properties: Store instance-specific IDs as properties and reference them dynamically. This allows safe changes per environment without editing code.
  • Lookups by stable attributes: Use unique human-readable fields (e.g., name, short_name, code) and add unique indexes where needed.
  • Configuration tables: For complex mappings (e.g., process to group), use dedicated configuration tables instead of sprinkling sys_ids across Script Includes.

Using System Properties for Upgrade-Safe Behavior

System properties are one of the most powerful tools for keeping custom logic upgrade-safe. They turn hard-coded decisions into configuration.

Patterns for property-driven behavior

  • Feature toggles: Gate new logic behind a boolean property so you can switch behavior on or off without code changes during or after an upgrade.
  • Thresholds and limits: Keep timeouts, retry counts, and size limits in properties; tuning them later becomes trivial.
  • Environment-specific values: URLs, email addresses, or group names should rarely be hard-coded in logic.

Code example 3: Property-driven configuration and safe lookup

var EscalationEngine = Class.create();
EscalationEngine.prototype = {
    initialize: function() {
        this.escalationGroupCode = gs.getProperty(
            'x_app.escalation.group_code', 'L2_ESC'
        );
    },

    getEscalationGroup: function() {
        var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user_group');
        gr.addQuery('u_code', this.escalationGroupCode);
        gr.setLimit(1);
        gr.query();
        if (gr.next())
            return gr.sys_id.toString();

        gs.error('EscalationEngine: group not found for code {0}',
            this.escalationGroupCode);
        return '';
    },

    escalateIncident: function(incidentGr) {
        if (!incidentGr || !incidentGr.isValidRecord())
            return;

        var groupId = this.getEscalationGroup();
        if (!groupId)
            return;

        incidentGr.assignment_group = groupId;
        incidentGr.update();
    },

    type: 'EscalationEngine'
};

The instance-specific mapping between escalation logic and group is in a property and a configured code field, not a sys_id. If the group changes, admins update configuration, not code, preserving upgrade safety.

Safe Refactoring During and Between Upgrades

Refactoring is often necessary as your implementation evolves and OOB features improve. Done carefully, it can reduce future upgrade load instead of increasing it.

Safe refactoring practices

  • Introduce adapters, then switch callers: Wrap legacy logic in a Script Include and change callers to use the wrapper before you rewrite the internals.
  • Keep public behavior stable: Preserve method names, signatures, and return shapes while you change internals. Add new behavior via optional parameters or new methods, not breaking changes.
  • Use feature flags for major changes: For large behavior shifts, deploy with a property toggle. Validate in lower instances and cut over gradually.
  • Align with OOB patterns: Whenever an upgrade adds a standard feature overlapping with your customization, favor refactors that delegate to OOB logic rather than maintaining parallel implementations.

Common Anti-Patterns to Avoid

Recognizing anti-patterns makes it easier to spot future upgrade risks in code reviews.

  • Fat Business Rules: Hundreds of lines of logic directly in a Business Rule with no Script Includes. This is hard to merge with OOB changes and hard to test.
  • Unbounded GlideRecord queries: Queries with missing filters, unchecked parameters, or no limits, leading to performance risks that surface under new releases or data growth.
  • Hard-coded sys_ids and magic numbers: sys_ids, state values, duration thresholds, and group names embedded in logic instead of properties or configuration tables.
  • Copy-paste logic across artifacts: The same complex snippet replicated across multiple Business Rules, UI Actions, and Script Includes. This multiplies upgrade effort and defect risk.
  • Direct modification of OOB Script Includes without wrappers: Editing base system classes directly instead of extending or wrapping them increases conflict frequency and reduces clarity during compare/resolve in upgrades.

Conclusion

Upgrade-safe scripting in ServiceNow is less about individual clever tricks and more about disciplined patterns: keep logic encapsulated in Script Includes, write defensive and bounded GlideRecord queries, avoid hard-coded sys_ids through properties and configuration, and refactor via small, behavior-preserving steps. By following these practices consistently, you reduce upgrade conflicts, improve maintainability, and give your organization the confidence to adopt new platform releases quickly and safely.

title: Designing Secure ServiceNow Applications: From ACLs to Threat Modeling
excerpt: A deep dive into secure development on the Now Platform, focusing on ACL evaluation, role design, scoped application boundaries, GlideRecord security, and preventing data leaks. Includes a lightweight threat model and two practical code examples you can reuse in real projects.
content:
Overview

Secure development on the Now Platform is much more than turning on the High Security plugin or adding a few ACLs. It requires a disciplined approach to access control, role modeling, scoped application design, secure scripting with GlideRecord, and continuous defense against data leaks. This article walks through a practical, developer-focused view of these areas and closes with a concise threat-model style section you can adapt to your own applications.

While platform features such as TLS, encryption at rest, MFA, and Security Center are essential, many real incidents originate in custom application logic and misconfigured access controls. As a ServiceNow developer, the most impactful controls you design are often in your own tables, scripts, and roles.

ACL Evaluation: Getting Access Control Right

Every record and field access in ServiceNow flows through Access Control Lists (ACLs). The core rules to keep in mind:

  • Default deny: If no ACL explicitly grants access, the platform denies it. This is your safety net only if you do not weaken it with broad allow rules.
  • Table, field, and script conditions must all pass: For a user to read a field, the table-level and field-level ACLs for that operation (read, write, create, delete) must all evaluate to true.
  • Order of evaluation: ServiceNow evaluates role, condition, and script elements; one failure is enough to block access. Layout convenience (like form design) never overrides ACLs.

Practical guidelines for ACLs:

  • Prefer role + condition combinations over heavy script logic. Scripted ACLs are powerful but harder to reason about, test, and audit.
  • Use field-level ACLs for sensitive columns such as personal data, secrets, or internal-only attributes, even if the table itself is widely accessible.
  • Avoid catch-all ACLs that rely on admin or a single broad role for many tables. They make access reviews and incident investigations difficult.
  • Test ACLs using impersonation and the Security Admin tools rather than assuming group/role mappings are correct.

Code example: A secure, reusable ACL script include

Instead of embedding complex logic directly in an ACL script, centralize it in a Script Include that you can unit test and reuse across multiple ACLs:

var SecureProjectAccess = Class.create();
SecureProjectAccess.prototype = {
    initialize: function() {},

    canReadProject: function(current) {
        // Only allow members, owners, or security officers
        if (gs.hasRole('sn_proj.security_officer'))
            return true;

        var userId = gs.getUserID();
        if (current.owner == userId)
            return true;

        var gr = new GlideRecord('u_project_member');
        gr.addQuery('u_project', current.sys_id);
        gr.addQuery('u_user', userId);
        gr.setLimit(1);
        gr.query();
        return gr.hasNext();
    },

    type: 'SecureProjectAccess'
};

You then call new SecureProjectAccess().canReadProject(current) from the ACL script field, ensuring that any later logic change is made in one place and can be regression-tested.

Role Design: Modeling Least Privilege

Roles are the backbone of ServiceNow’s role-based access control (RBAC) model. Sloppy role design quickly erodes even well-written ACLs. A secure design follows these principles:

  • Least privilege: Define roles for specific job functions (e.g., sn_app.request_approver) rather than generic power-user roles that accumulate unrelated permissions.
  • Layered roles: Use small, composable roles (e.g., base reader, editor, approver) and then aggregate them into application-level roles or groups. This aids reviews and onboarding.
  • Separation of duties: Avoid roles that mix conflicting powers, such as configuring approval rules and approving their own requests.
  • No hidden dependencies: Document what each role enables (tables, modules, script actions). Hidden role inheritance chains are fertile ground for misunderstandings and privilege escalation.

Review roles regularly with security and process owners, focusing on who can export data, impersonate, modify ACLs, or change business rules.

Scoped Application Boundaries

Scoped applications are a primary way to isolate business logic and data from the rest of the instance. A secure design uses scopes intentionally, not just for namespace convenience.

  • Limit cross-scope access: Only grant cross-scope privileges (e.g., Allow access to this table from other scopes) when there is a clear need. Broad cross-scope APIs weaken isolation.
  • Explicit public APIs: For shared logic, expose Script Includes as accessible from other scopes, but keep internal helpers private. Treat these public includes as versioned, documented APIs.
  • Control table visibility: Use scope and ACLs together so that only your app’s roles, not global ones, control access to app data tables.
  • ATF and regression tests: Include automated tests verifying that unauthorized scopes cannot create, modify, or read your scoped tables.

Effective scope boundaries reduce the blast radius when a single application has a defect or misconfiguration.

GlideRecord Security and Safe Querying

Any custom script that uses GlideRecord is a potential bypass of UI-layer controls. To keep GlideRecord usage secure:

  • Never assume UI conditions enforce security: Always add explicit query conditions in server-side scripts (Business Rules, Script Includes, Scheduled Jobs, Flow Actions).
  • Filter by user context: Where appropriate, constrain queries by the current user, their company, or a security tag instead of pulling broad datasets.
  • Beware of system contexts: Scripts running with elevated privileges (e.g., background scripts, Fix Scripts, some integrations) can ignore ACLs. Treat these as sensitive operations.
  • Limit result sets: Use setLimit() and targeted queries to prevent accidental mass reads or exports, especially in integrations.

Code example: Secure record retrieval with GlideRecord

This example shows a Script Include method that enforces both ACL-style checks and tight queries for a scoped app service API:

var SecureIncidentService = Class.create();
SecureIncidentService.prototype = {
    initialize: function() {},

    getUserIncidents: function() {
        var userId = gs.getUserID();
        var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
        gr.addActiveQuery();
        gr.addQuery('caller_id', userId);
        gr.setLimit(50);
        gr.query();

        var results = [];
        while (gr.next()) {
            // Return only non-sensitive fields to the caller
            results.push({
                number: gr.getValue('number'),
                short_description: gr.getValue('short_description'),
                state: gr.getDisplayValue('state')
            });
        }
        return results;
    },

    type: 'SecureIncidentService'
};

Note that this method does not expose fields like work notes or security classification and constrains the query to the current user with a sensible limit.

Preventing Data Leaks

Many ServiceNow data leaks originate from legitimate functionality used in unsafe ways rather than from outright exploitation. Focus protection where bulk or sensitive data can escape:

  • Exports and reports: Restrict who can export to Excel/CSV or schedule reports. Scrutinize roles that can build reports over sensitive tables.
  • Email and notifications: Avoid including full records or sensitive fields in outbound emails. Prefer links back to the instance and ACL-protected views.
  • APIs and integrations: Use OAuth or mutual TLS, scope tokens narrowly, and design API responses to include only necessary fields.
  • Attachments: Treat attachments as potentially sensitive. Limit who can download or upload on sensitive tables and monitor large attachment traffic.
  • Encryption and masking: Use platform encryption features for confidential fields and masking in logs where possible, especially for credentials and personal data.

Combine these with monitoring and audit logs to detect unusual export volumes, new high-privilege integrations, or sudden role changes.

Threat-Model Style View for a ServiceNow App

You can apply a lightweight threat model to each application to systematically discover risks. Here is a concise structure tailored to ServiceNow development:

1. Assets

  • Business records (e.g., incidents, HR cases, financial approvals)
  • Personal data (names, contact details, identifiers)
  • Configuration and security metadata (ACLs, roles, business rules)
  • Integration credentials and secrets

2. Entry points

  • UI (forms, lists, Service Portal, Workspaces)
  • REST/SOAP APIs and scripted web services
  • Email inbound actions
  • Integrations via MID Server or external tools
  • Admin and delegated admin interfaces

3. Key threats

  • Excessive data exposure: Over-broad ACLs, exports, or API responses allow users to see data outside their function.
  • Privilege escalation: Misconfigured roles or group memberships grant admin-like capabilities.
  • Cross-scope abuse: Another app calls your public scripts or tables in unexpected ways.
  • Bypassing business logic: Scripts with elevated contexts or direct table APIs ignore workflow constraints or approvals.
  • Injection and unsafe scripting: Poor input validation in scripts or dynamic query building leads to unexpected behavior.

4. Mitigations

  • Define and enforce ACLs for every sensitive table and field, using reusable Script Includes where logic is complex.
  • Design roles around business functions, periodically reviewing them for least privilege and separation of duties.
  • Use scoped app boundaries with minimal cross-scope grants and clearly documented public APIs.
  • Constrain GlideRecord queries by user and context, limit result sets, and avoid unnecessary fields in APIs and exports.
  • Enable and review auditing, security logs, and configuration changes, feeding high-value events into your SIEM.

Conclusion

Secure development on the Now Platform is a continuous practice that starts with clear access control, thoughtful role and scope design, and disciplined use of GlideRecord. When you combine these with careful handling of exports, emails, and APIs—and regularly walk through a simple threat model for each app—you significantly reduce the chance of data leaks and privilege issues, while still delivering powerful, maintainable ServiceNow solutions.

title: Practical Guide to ServiceNow AI: Now Assist, Predictive Intelligence, and Virtual Agent
excerpt: A concise, practical look at ServiceNow's core AI features—Now Assist, Predictive Intelligence, and Virtual Agent—with two simple code examples to help you connect the concepts to real platform work.
content:
Overview

ServiceNow's AI portfolio revolves around three core experiences: Now Assist for generative AI, Predictive Intelligence for machine learning–based classification and routing, and Virtual Agent for conversational self-service. Together, they help technical teams streamline work, boost agent productivity, and improve user satisfaction without replacing the existing platform foundations.

As a ServiceNow technical writer, understanding how these pieces fit together is essential for explaining not just features, but end-to-end AI-enhanced workflows.

Now Assist: GenAI in the Flow of Work

Now Assist brings generative AI directly into workspaces and builders' tools. It uses ServiceNow's Now LLM and integrated large language models to summarize records and conversations, draft content, and assist developers.

  • Summarization: Condenses cases, incidents, and long chat transcripts so agents can ramp up quickly.
  • Knowledge and email drafting: Generates knowledge article drafts, case updates, and customer responses from existing record context.
  • Developer assistance: Suggests code and Flow Designer logic, speeding up configuration and development cycles.
  • AI-enhanced search: Surfaces concise, contextual answers rather than only a list of knowledge articles.

In practice, Now Assist turns the platform into a context-aware assistant that helps users consume and produce information faster while staying within established governance.

Predictive Intelligence: Routing, Classification, and Forecasting

Predictive Intelligence uses traditional machine learning to classify and route records based on historical data. It excels at repetitive, high-volume tasks that follow recognizable patterns.

  • Automated routing: Predicts assignment group or resolver team for incidents, cases, and requests.
  • Categorization and prioritization: Suggests category, subcategory, and priority values to reduce manual data entry.
  • Trend prediction: Helps forecast volumes or detect anomalies when combined with analytics and performance dashboards.

For many implementations, Predictive Intelligence is the backbone of AI-driven workflows, with Now Assist layered on top for natural-language generation and summarization.

Code example: Using GlideRecord with an AI-routed table

This simple snippet shows a standard server-side pattern you might use in a business rule or script include that runs after Predictive Intelligence has populated routing fields:

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addNullQuery('assignment_group');
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  if (gr.u_predicted_group) {
    gr.assignment_group = gr.u_predicted_group;
    gr.update();
  }
}

The logic is conventional GlideRecord scripting; the AI value is in the predicted field that your model maintains.

Virtual Agent: Conversational Self-Service

Virtual Agent provides an NLU-driven chatbot interface that handles routine questions and requests via web, mobile, and collaboration tools. It is tightly integrated with Flow Designer and the Service Catalog.

  • 24/7 self-service for common requests like password resets, access requests, and status checks.
  • Intent detection and slot filling using NLU models mapped to topics.
  • Process automation via flows and subflows, so conversations trigger real work in the platform.
  • Escalation to live agent with full context when the bot cannot resolve an issue.

Code example: Simple record lookup behind a Virtual Agent topic

Behind a Virtual Agent topic, you often call Scripted REST APIs or Script Includes. The following GlideRecord pattern could power a Check my incident status step:

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('number', vaInputs.incident_number);
gr.addQuery('caller_id', gs.getUserID());
gr.query();
if (gr.next()) {
  vaOutputs.status = gr.state.getDisplayValue();
  vaOutputs.short_description = gr.short_description;
} else {
  vaOutputs.error = 'No matching incident found.';
}

This code exposes only what the Virtual Agent topic needs (status and short description), while respecting caller context and security.

Bringing It All Together

Individually, Now Assist, Predictive Intelligence, and Virtual Agent solve different problems, but their real value appears when you combine them into a single experience: Predictive Intelligence routes and enriches records, Virtual Agent handles front-door conversations, and Now Assist accelerates agents and developers working behind the scenes. As you document these capabilities, focus on how each feature enhances existing workflows and how they can be composed into end-to-end AI journeys for your stakeholders.

title: Automating ServiceNow ITSM with a Healthy CMDB and Optimized Workflows
excerpt: Learn how to combine CMDB best practices with workflow automation in ServiceNow ITSM to drive reliable, scalable operations. This article covers data quality, relationships, and Flow Designer patterns, plus two code examples for CMDB and incident automation.
content:
Overview

ServiceNow ITSM automation delivers its best results only when it is grounded in a clean, reliable Configuration Management Database (CMDB) and well-designed workflows. A healthy CMDB provides trustworthy data for impact analysis, routing, and reporting, while optimized flows remove manual steps and reduce resolution times. This article outlines practical CMDB best practices and workflow patterns that technical writers, admins, and developers can use to describe and implement scalable automation.

CMDB Best Practices for Automation

The CMDB is the foundation for impact-driven ITSM. When configuration items (CIs) and relationships are accurate, automation can safely drive assignments, escalations, and change decisions without constant human checks.

  • Define a clear data model: Document which CI classes you will use, the mandatory attributes for each, and how they relate (for example, Business Service Application Server). Keep the model as simple as possible while still supporting incident, problem, and change processes.
  • Standardize CI sources: Use Discovery, Service Mapping, and integration patterns to reduce manual CI creation. Centralizing data ingestion cuts down duplicates and inconsistent naming that can break automated routing or impact analysis.
  • Enforce data quality: Implement CI lifecycle workflows, UI policies, and data policies to validate ownership, support group, environment, and criticality. Poorly populated fields lead to misrouted incidents and noisy impact calculations.
  • Maintain relationships: Automations that determine impact, change risk, or escalation paths depend on accurate CI relationships. Treat relationships as first-class data: document them, review them regularly, and validate them during change implementations.
  • Governance and ongoing maintenance: Create ownership for CI classes and establish regular audits, dashboards, and reports that highlight stale CIs, missing relationships, and orphan records. Automation quality follows CMDB quality.

CMDB-Focused Automation Example

The following script example shows how you might automatically set an incident's assignment group based on its affected CI. This logic can be embedded in a Business Rule or Flow Designer action:

// Prefer using current in a Business Rule; shown as a standalone pattern
var inc = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (inc.get(current.getUniqueValue()) && inc.cmdb_ci) {
  var ci = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci');
  if (ci.get(inc.cmdb_ci) && ci.support_group) {
    inc.assignment_group = ci.support_group;
    inc.update();
  }
}

This type of automation keeps assignment logic centralized in the CMDB instead of scattering group rules across multiple workflows.

Workflow Optimization in ServiceNow ITSM

With a strong CMDB in place, ServiceNow workflows and Flow Designer can automate request, incident, and change processes end-to-end. Good design keeps flows maintainable and resilient over time.

  • Start from the process: Document current-state steps, pain points, handoffs, and decision points before building flows. Automation should remove friction, not replicate inefficient manual steps in code.
  • Use modular subflows: Break large processes into reusable subflows for notifications, approvals, and CI-based impact checks. This increases reuse and reduces regression risk when requirements change.
  • Leverage decision tables: For complex routing or approval logic, decision tables are easier to maintain than deeply nested if/else branches. Non-developers can safely adjust rules without editing scripts.
  • Minimize custom script: Prefer out-of-the-box actions, data pills, and configuration over large Script steps. When scripting is required, keep it small, well-commented, and constrained to specific tasks.
  • Implement robust error handling: Use error handlers, logging, and notifications for integration failures, missing data, or SLA breaches so workflows fail gracefully and are easier to troubleshoot.

Workflow Automation Example

The script below illustrates a basic pattern to automatically escalate high-priority incidents that approach their SLA breach time. It can be called from a Scheduled Script Execution or a Flow Designer Script step.

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
gr.addQuery('state', '!=', 6);
gr.addQuery('u_minutes_to_breach', '<=', 30);
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  gr.setWorkflow(false);
  gr.assignment_group = 'P1_ESCALATION_GROUP_SYS_ID';
  gr.u_escalated = true;
  gr.update();
}

This pattern demonstrates how workflow logic can use CMDB-backed data and SLA metrics to trigger timely, consistent escalations without manual monitoring.

Conclusion

Effective ServiceNow ITSM automation depends on a clean, governed CMDB and workflow designs that are modular, rule-driven, and resilient. By investing in CMDB data quality, centralizing routing and impact logic on CIs, and using Flow Designer patterns like subflows, decision tables, and targeted scripting, organizations can safely scale automation while maintaining control, transparency, and auditability.

title: Mastering ServiceNow Core APIs: GlideRecord, GlideAggregate, and RESTMessageV2
excerpt: A practical walkthrough of three core ServiceNow APIs—GlideRecord, GlideAggregate, and RESTMessageV2—with clear use cases and code you can reuse in your own instance.
content:
Overview

ServiceNow's core server-side APIs are the backbone of most customizations and integrations. As a technical writer and developer, understanding how to explain and apply GlideRecord, GlideAggregate, and RESTMessageV2 is essential for building reliable, scalable solutions on the Now Platform.

This article focuses on practical usage. We will cover when to use each API and walk through three simple, reusable code examples you can adapt in your own instance.

GlideRecord: Core CRUD and Query Operations

GlideRecord is the primary server-side API for interacting with ServiceNow tables. Use it whenever you need to create, read, update, or delete records directly from scripts such as Business Rules, Script Includes, or Scheduled Jobs.

Typical use cases include:

  • Querying incidents that match specific conditions
  • Bulk updating records (for example, closing old tasks)
  • Creating new records with defaulted values

Example 1: Query and update active incidents

The following pattern retrieves active incidents with a given priority and updates their work notes. It is suitable for a Background Script or Scheduled Job.

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.addQuery('priority', 2);
gr.query();

while (gr.next()) {
  gr.work_notes = 'Reviewed by nightly maintenance job.';
  gr.update();
}

This example demonstrates the standard lifecycle: instantiate GlideRecord, add query conditions, execute query(), loop with next(), and persist changes with update().

GlideAggregate: Efficient Aggregation at Scale

GlideAggregate is optimized for aggregate database operations such as counts, sums, minimums, and maximums. Use it instead of looping through large result sets when you only need statistics.

Common use cases include:

  • Reporting counts of records by category or state
  • Calculating totals (for example, total hours on tasks)
  • Building quick KPIs in server-side logic

Example 2: Count active incidents by category

This example counts active incidents grouped by category, a typical KPI pattern you can reuse in Script Includes or server-side widgets.

var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
ga.addQuery('active', true);
ga.groupBy('category');
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.query();

while (ga.next()) {
  var category = ga.category;
  var count = ga.getAggregate('COUNT');
  gs.info('Active incidents in category ' + category + ': ' + count);
}

By pushing the aggregation into the database, GlideAggregate reduces memory usage and improves performance compared to iterating over full GlideRecord result sets.

RESTMessageV2: Calling External APIs from ServiceNow

RESTMessageV2 is the primary API for outbound REST calls from ServiceNow. Use it to integrate with third-party systems, internal microservices, or other ServiceNow instances.

Typical use cases include:

  • Creating or updating records in external tools (for example, Jira or monitoring platforms)
  • Fetching reference data from internal APIs
  • Triggering external workflows from ServiceNow events

Example 3: Simple outbound POST with RESTMessageV2

The following script sends incident data to an external endpoint. In production, you would usually back this with an Outbound REST Message configuration, but inline usage is helpful for prototypes and background scripts.

var rm = new RESTMessageV2();
rm.setHttpMethod('post');
rm.setEndpoint('https://api.example.com/incidents');

var payload = {
  number: current.number.toString(),
  short_description: current.short_description.toString(),
  priority: current.priority.toString()
};

rm.setRequestHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
rm.setRequestBody(JSON.stringify(payload));

var response = rm.execute();
var status = response.getStatusCode();
var body = response.getBody();

gs.info('External API status: ' + status + ', response: ' + body);

This example highlights the core steps: define method and endpoint, construct a JSON payload, set headers, execute, and inspect the response for logging or error handling.

Conclusion

GlideRecord, GlideAggregate, and RESTMessageV2 form the foundation of most server-side logic on the Now Platform. GlideRecord handles core CRUD operations, GlideAggregate provides efficient reporting and KPIs, and RESTMessageV2 enables integrations with the wider ecosystem. By mastering the patterns in these three examples, you can confidently design, document, and implement robust solutions across your ServiceNow environment.

title: JS for ServiceNow: 1. Introduction

content:
Welcome to Your JavaScript Journey

Whether you're an HR analyst automating leave calculations, an IT service desk manager building incident workflows, or a finance professional streamlining approvals—this tutorial series will transform you into a confident ServiceNow developer.

What makes this series different? We teach through the lens of real interview scenarios, show you exactly how code executes line by line, and give you working examples you can use immediately.

Why Server-Side First?

ServiceNow JavaScript differs fundamentally from web JavaScript. The platform's architecture demands a specific learning path. We start with GlideRecord because it's the gateway to everything else—once you master querying data, every other concept builds naturally.

💡 The Golden Rule: GlideRecord → Business Rules → Script Includes → GlideAjax. Never skip ahead. Each concept depends on the previous one.

The Learning Path

PhaseTopicsWhy This Order
Weeks 1-2JS Fundamentals + Platform BasicsFoundation for everything
Weeks 3-4GlideRecord + GlideSystem APIsCore database operations
Weeks 5-6Business Rules (before, after, async)Most important server script

How Each Tutorial Works

Every lesson follows the PRIMM framework—a research-backed approach that dramatically improves retention:

1. Interview Scenario

🎯 SCENARIO: Your organization's Incident Management team reports that high-priority incidents assigned to inactive users remain unaddressed for days.

BUSINESS CONTEXT: User accounts become inactive when employees leave, but incidents may still reference them as assignees.

YOUR TASK: Write a Business Rule that automatically reassigns incidents from inactive users to the assignment group's manager.

2. Code Walkthrough with Labeled Steps

// === STEP 1: CHECK TRIGGER CONDITION ===
if (current.state == 6) {  // Resolved state
    
    // === STEP 2: VALIDATE REQUIRED DATA ===
    if (gs.nil(current.assignment_group)) {

    }

}

For Non-Programmers: The Spreadsheet Bridge

Think of GlideRecord as a "database formula"—just like Excel formulas filter and transform data:

Excel ConceptServiceNow Equivalent

title: JS for ServiceNow: 2. GlideRecord Basics
excerpt: Master the most important API in ServiceNow. Learn to query, create, update, and delete records with real interview scenarios and execution traces.
content:
The Foundation of Everything

GlideRecord is the single most important skill for ServiceNow development and the primary API for server-side database operations. It enables querying, creating, updating, and deleting records across any table, making it the core interface between your scripts and the ServiceNow database.

The GlideRecord API is a server-side JavaScript object that represents records from tables like incident, problem, or sys_user. It provides methods to add query conditions, execute database hits, iterate results, and perform CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete). Unlike client-side scripting, this API runs on the server for secure, efficient data access.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "Write a script that finds all active high-priority incidents assigned to the 'Network' group and updates their state to 'In Progress' if they've been open for more than 24 hours."

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Query construction, date comparisons, efficient updates, and understanding of when conditions.

GlideRecord API Overview

The GlideRecord API supports both global and scoped applications. In global scope, use new GlideRecord('table_name'). In scoped apps, it respects application access controls. Key categories include:

  • Query Methods: addQuery(), addEncodedQuery(), query(), get()
  • CRUD Methods: initialize(), insert(), update(), deleteRecord(), deleteMultiple()
  • Iteration Methods: next(), hasNext()
  • Utility Methods: setValue(), getValue(), setLimit()

Basic Query Pattern

Every GlideRecord interaction follows: Create → Configure → Query → Iterate.

// === CREATE: Initialize GlideRecord on a table ===
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');

// === CONFIGURE: Add your conditions ===
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
gr.addQuery('assignment_group', 'Network Group Sys ID');
// Open for more than 24 hours

gr.addQuery('sys_created_on', '<=', gs.hoursAgoStart(24));

// === QUERY: Execute the database query ===
gr.query();

// === ITERATE: Loop through results ===
while (gr.next()) {
  gr.setValue('state', 2); // In Progress
  gr.update();
  gs.info('Updated: ' + gr.getValue('number'));
}

Execution Trace

StepWhat HappensDatabase Impact
new GlideRecord('incident')Creates object pointing to incident tableNone yet
addQuery(...)Builds WHERE conditionsNone yet
query()Executes SELECT with your conditionsDatabase hit
next()Moves pointer to next recordNone
update()Persists changeDatabase write

The get() Shortcut

Use get() for single records by sys_id or unique field—it's faster than query() for one record.

// By sys_id (most common)
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (gr.get('a1b2c3d4e5f6...')) {
  gs.info('Found: ' + gr.getValue('number'));
}

// By any unique field
var userGr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
if (userGr.get('user_name', 'admin')) {
  gs.info('Admin sys_id: ' + userGr.getUniqueValue());
}

Creating Records

The GlideRecord API's insert() method creates new records after setting fields via initialize() and setValue().

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.initialize();
gr.setValue('short_description', 'Network outage in Building A');
gr.setValue('category', 'network');
gr.setValue('priority', 2);
var newSysId = gr.insert();

gs.info('Created incident: ' + newSysId);

Updating Records

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (gr.get('number', 'INC0010001')) {
  gr.setValue('state', 2);
  gr.setValue('assigned_to', gs.getUserID());
  gr.update();
}

Deleting Records

deleteRecord() removes the current record; deleteMultiple() bulk-deletes matching ones.

// Delete single record
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (gr.get('sys_id_here')) {
  gr.deleteRecord();
}

// Delete multiple records
var gr2 = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr2.addQuery('state', 7);
gr2.addQuery('sys_created_on', '<', gs.daysAgo(365));
gr2.deleteMultiple();

Essential Query Operators

OperatorExampleMeaning
=addQuery('priority', 1)Equals
!=addQuery('state', '!=', 6)Not equals
>addQuery('priority', '>', 2)Greater than
INaddQuery('state', 'IN', '1,2,3')In list
CONTAINSaddQuery('short_description', 'CONTAINS', 'network')Contains text
ISEMPTYaddQuery('assigned_to', 'ISEMPTY')Field is empty

Performance: setLimit()

💡 Always use setLimit() when you only need a few records:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.setLimit(10);
gr.query();
This prevents querying millions of records and improves performance.

Advanced GlideRecord API Features

Key methods include addEncodedQuery() for complex filters, clearQuery() to reset conditions, and hasNext() for pre-checking results.

// Complex encoded query
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addEncodedQuery('active=true^priority=1^sys_created_on<javascript:gs.daysAgo(1)');
gr.query();
while (gr.hasNext()) {
  gr.next();
  gs.print(gr.getValue('number'));
}

Challenge: Put It All Together

🏋️ CHALLENGE: Write a script that:
1. Finds all incidents in "New" state (state=1)
2. Open for more than 48 hours (use gs.hoursAgoStart(48))
3. No assigned user (assigned_to ISEMPTY)
4. Updates priority to 2 (High)

Solution:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('state', 1);
gr.addQuery('sys_created_on', '<=', gs.hoursAgoStart(48));
gr.addQuery('assigned_to', 'ISEMPTY');
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  gr.setValue('priority', 2);
  gr.update();
}

Mastering the GlideRecord API unlocks efficient database interactions in ServiceNow, from background scripts to business rules.

title: JS for ServiceNow: 3. Business Rules
excerpt: Learn when and how to use Business Rules effectively. Understand before vs after rules, avoid common pitfalls, and master the 'current' and 'previous' objects.
content:
The Heart of Server-Side Logic

Business Rules are scripts that run when records are inserted, updated, deleted, or queried. They're the most powerful—and most commonly misused—server-side scripting tool in ServiceNow.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "An incident's priority should automatically escalate to P1 if it remains unassigned for more than 4 hours. How would you implement this?"

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Understanding of rule timing, when to use scheduled jobs vs business rules, and efficient database operations.

When Do Business Rules Run?

TypeWhen It RunsUse Case
BeforeBefore record is saved to databaseValidate data, set default values, modify current record
AfterAfter record is saved to databaseUpdate related records, send notifications, create tasks
AsyncAfter save, in backgroundHeavy processing, external API calls
DisplayWhen form loads (query)Set up client-side variables (g_scratchpad)

The 'current' and 'previous' Objects

// 'current' = the record being saved (with new values)
// 'previous' = the record before changes (read-only)

// Example: Detect if priority changed
if (current.priority.changesTo(1)) {
  gs.info('Priority escalated to P1!');
}

// Example: Detect any change to a field
if (current.state.changes()) {
  gs.info('State changed from ' + previous.state + ' to ' + current.state);
}

Execution Trace: Before Rule

Stepcurrent.stateprevious.stateDatabase
User clicks Save3 (new value)1 (old value)Still has 1
Before rule runs31Still has 1
Rule modifies currentModified1Still has 1
After rule completes--NOW saves current

Before Rule Example: Auto-Set Assignment Group

🎯 SCENARIO: When a user selects a Category of "Network", automatically set the Assignment Group to "Network Support".
// Business Rule: Auto-assign Network Incidents
// Table: incident
// When: before insert, before update
// Condition: current.category.changesTo('network')

(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  var groupGr = new GlideRecord('sys_user_group');
  groupGr.addQuery('name', 'Network Support');
  groupGr.query();

  if (groupGr.next()) {
    current.assignment_group = groupGr.getUniqueValue();
  }
})(current, previous);

After Rule Example: Create Follow-up Task

🎯 SCENARIO: When an incident is resolved, automatically create a follow-up task for customer satisfaction survey.
// Business Rule: Create Survey Task on Resolution
// Table: incident
// When: after update
// Condition: current.state.changesTo(6)

(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  var task = new GlideRecord('task');
  task.initialize();
  task.short_description = 'Customer survey for ' + current.number;
  task.parent = current.getUniqueValue();
  task.assigned_to = current.assigned_to;
  task.description = 'Please contact customer to complete satisfaction survey.';
  task.insert();

  gs.info('Created follow-up task for ' + current.number);
})(current, previous);

Condition Field vs Script Conditions

ApproachWhen to Use
Condition field: current.priority == 1Simple field comparisons
Script: if (complexLogic()) {...}Multiple conditions, lookups, calculations
💡 Performance Tip: Put as much logic as possible in the Condition field. It's evaluated before the script even loads, saving processing time when conditions aren't met.

Preventing Recursion

// Use setWorkflow(false) to prevent Business Rules from triggering on your update
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (gr.get(relatedIncidentId)) {
  gr.setWorkflow(false);
  gr.autoSysFields(false);
  gr.setValue('state', 6);
  gr.update();
}

Business Rules are the workhorse of ServiceNow automation. Master them, and you'll unlock the platform's true power.

title: JS for ServiceNow: 4. Script Includes
excerpt: Build reusable code libraries with Script Includes. Learn the difference between classless and class-based includes, and when to use client-callable scripts.
content:
Write Once, Use Everywhere

Script Includes are reusable server-side code libraries. Instead of copying the same code into multiple Business Rules, you write it once in a Script Include and call it from anywhere.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "Your team has the same incident validation logic duplicated across 5 Business Rules. How would you refactor this?"

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Understanding of code reusability, Script Include patterns, and maintainability best practices.

Two Common Styles of Script Includes

1) Class-Based (Recommended for most production use)

// Script Include: IncidentHelper
// Accessible from: Server-side only

var IncidentHelper = Class.create();
IncidentHelper.prototype = {
  initialize: function(incidentGr) {
    this.incident = incidentGr;
  },

  isHighPriority: function() {
    return parseInt(this.incident.getValue('priority'), 10) <= 2;
  },

  getAssignmentGroupName: function() {
    var group = this.incident.assignment_group.getRefRecord();
    return group.isValidRecord() ? group.getValue('name') : 'Unassigned';
  },

  escalate: function(reason) {
    this.incident.setValue('priority', 1);
    this.incident.setValue('work_notes', 'Escalated: ' + reason);
    return this.incident.update();
  },

  type: 'IncidentHelper'
};

Usage in Business Rule:

var helper = new IncidentHelper(current);
if (helper.isHighPriority() && current.assigned_to.nil()) {
  helper.escalate('High priority and unassigned');
}

2) Simple Utility (Ok for small helpers)

// Script Include: IncidentUtils
// Pattern: expose a single object with functions

var IncidentUtils = {
  isVIPUser: function(userId) {
    var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
    return gr.get(userId) && gr.getValue('vip') == 'true';
  },

  getActiveIncidentCount: function(userId) {
    var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
    ga.addQuery('assigned_to', userId);
    ga.addQuery('active', true);
    ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
    ga.query();
    return ga.next() ? parseInt(ga.getAggregate('COUNT'), 10) : 0;
  }
};

Client-Callable Script Includes (GlideAjax)

When you mark a Script Include as Client callable, it is typically written by extending AbstractAjaxProcessor. Client scripts call named methods using sysparm_name and parameters using sysparm_*.

// Script Include: UserUtilsAjax
// Client callable: true

var UserUtilsAjax = Class.create();
UserUtilsAjax.prototype = Object.extendsObject(AbstractAjaxProcessor, {
  getUserEmail: function() {
    var userId = this.getParameter('sysparm_user_id');
    var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
    return (gr.get(userId) && gr.email) ? gr.getValue('email') : '';
  },

  type: 'UserUtilsAjax'
});

Client Script Usage:

var ga = new GlideAjax('UserUtilsAjax');
ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getUserEmail');
ga.addParam('sysparm_user_id', g_form.getValue('caller_id'));
ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
  g_form.setValue('u_caller_email', answer);
});

Best Practices for Script Includes

  • Single Responsibility: Each Script Include should do one thing well
  • Validation: Validate inputs and return predictable outputs
  • Security: Keep client-callable includes minimal; enforce ACL-friendly access
  • Performance: Avoid repeated queries; cache where appropriate
  • Naming: Use clear names that describe behavior, not implementation

Script Includes are your foundation for writing maintainable, scalable ServiceNow code. Master this pattern and your development speed will multiply.

title: JS for ServiceNow: 5. GlideAjax and Client-Server Communication
excerpt: Learn how to communicate between client-side scripts and server-side code using GlideAjax. Understand asynchronous patterns and real-time data fetching.
content:
Bridge the Client-Server Gap

GlideAjax is ServiceNow's mechanism for making asynchronous calls from client-side scripts to server-side Script Includes. This is essential for real-time validations, lookups, and dynamic UI updates without page reloads.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "When a user selects a caller on an incident, you need to populate their email address, department, and manager name in real-time. How would you implement this without a page refresh?"

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Async patterns, callback functions, and understanding of client vs server scope.

The GlideAjax Pattern

Every GlideAjax call follows four steps: Create instance, Add parameters, Define callback, Execute.

Server-Side Script Include

// Script Include: CallerInfoAjax
// Client callable: true

var CallerInfoAjax = Class.create();
CallerInfoAjax.prototype = Object.extendsObject(AbstractAjaxProcessor, {
  getUserInfo: function() {
    var userId = this.getParameter('sysparm_user_id');
    var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
    if (gr.get(userId)) {
      var result = {
        email: gr.getValue('email'),
        department: gr.getDisplayValue('department'),
        manager: gr.getDisplayValue('manager'),
        phone: gr.getValue('phone')
      };
      return JSON.stringify(result);
    }
    return JSON.stringify({ error: 'User not found' });
  },

  type: 'CallerInfoAjax'
});

Client-Side onChange Script

// Client Script: onChange (caller_id)
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
  if (isLoading || !newValue) return;

  var ga = new GlideAjax('CallerInfoAjax');
  ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getUserInfo');
  ga.addParam('sysparm_user_id', newValue);

  ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
    var data = JSON.parse(answer || '{}');
    if (data.error) {
      g_form.showFieldMsg('caller_id', data.error, 'error');
      return;
    }

    g_form.setValue('u_caller_email', data.email || '');
    g_form.setValue('u_caller_dept', data.department || '');
    g_form.setValue('u_caller_manager', data.manager || '');
    g_form.setValue('u_caller_phone', data.phone || '');
  });
}

Execution Trace: GlideAjax Call

EventScopeWhat HappensTime
User changes callerClientonChange firesT+0ms
Create GlideAjaxClientRequest is preparedT+5ms
getXMLAnswer()ClientHTTP request sentT+10ms
Script Include runsServerReads sys_user and returns JSONT+50ms
Callback executesClientFields updatedT+100ms

Common GlideAjax Patterns

Pattern 1: Simple Lookup

var ga = new GlideAjax('SomeAjax');
ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'lookup');
ga.addParam('sysparm_key', 'value');
ga.getXMLAnswer(function(response) {
  // handle response
});

Pattern 2: With Error Handling

var ga = new GlideAjax('ValidationAjax');
ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'validate');
ga.addParam('sysparm_value', g_form.getValue('u_field'));

ga.getXMLAnswer(function(response) {
  if (response == 'ERROR') {
    g_form.showFieldMsg('u_field', 'Validation failed', 'error');
  }
});

GlideAjax is your gateway to creating responsive, real-time ServiceNow interfaces. Master this pattern for seamless user experiences.

title: JS for ServiceNow: 6. Advanced Optimization Patterns
excerpt: Learn performance optimization techniques including N+1 query prevention, caching strategies, and efficient bulk operations.
content:
Write Fast Code That Scales

The difference between code that works and code that scales is attention to performance. This section covers real patterns used in production ServiceNow instances handling millions of records.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "Your Business Rule that updates related incidents is causing database timeouts when processing 50,000 incidents daily. How would you optimize it?"

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Understanding of N+1 queries, batch processing, and GlideRecord efficiency.

Anti-Pattern: The N+1 Query Problem

Bad: This code queries incidents, then AGAIN for each incident's group:

// ❌ INEFFICIENT: N+1 Query
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.query();

while (gr.next()) {
  var groupGr = new GlideRecord('sys_user_group');
  groupGr.get(gr.assignment_group);
  gs.info('Incident ' + gr.number + ' assigned to ' + groupGr.name);
}
// Total hits: 1 + number of incidents

Solution: Caching

Good: Cache group names so each group is queried once:

// ✅ OPTIMIZED: Cached Lookups
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.query();

var groupCache = {};

while (gr.next()) {
  var groupId = gr.getValue('assignment_group');

  if (groupId && !groupCache[groupId]) {
    var groupGr = new GlideRecord('sys_user_group');
    if (groupGr.get(groupId)) {
      groupCache[groupId] = groupGr.getValue('name');
    }
  }

  gs.info('Incident ' + gr.getValue('number') + ' assigned to ' + (groupCache[groupId] || 'Unassigned'));
}

Bulk Operations: Know When updateMultiple Works

If you are setting the same value on many records, updateMultiple() is usually faster than looping.

// ✅ FAST: One update statement (same values for all matches)
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('priority', 5);
gr.setValue('priority', 3);
gr.updateMultiple();

Query Optimization: Essential Techniques

1. Use setLimit() for Large Tables

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.setLimit(1000);
gr.query();

2. Use orderBy() for Pagination

var pageSize = 100;
var offset = 0;

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.orderBy('sys_created_on');
gr.setSkip(offset);
gr.setLimit(pageSize);
gr.query();

3. Use addEncodedQuery() for Complex Filters

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addEncodedQuery('active=true^priority<=3^assignment_group!=NULL');
gr.query();

GlideAggregate for Reporting

Never use GlideRecord + loop for counting:

// ✅ GOOD: Database does the counting
var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
ga.addQuery('active', true);
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.query();
if (ga.next()) {
  gs.info('Total incidents: ' + ga.getAggregate('COUNT'));
}

Conclusion

Performance optimization in ServiceNow is mostly about reducing database hits, avoiding heavy loops, and choosing the right API for the job. Start by eliminating N+1 queries, then move to caching and bulk operations. Small fixes in one script can save minutes (or hours) across a day of platform load.

title: ServiceNow ITSM Automation: CMDB Best Practices and Workflow Optimization
excerpt: Discover essential best practices for automating ITSM in ServiceNow, focusing on maintaining an accurate CMDB for better decision-making and optimizing workflows with Flow Designer for efficiency.
content:
Introduction to ITSM Automation in ServiceNow

ServiceNow ITSM automation transforms IT service management by leveraging ITIL best practices, enabling organizations to streamline processes, reduce manual efforts, and enhance service delivery through tools like Flow Designer for workflow optimization and a well-maintained CMDB for informed decision-making.

CMDB Best Practices for ITSM Excellence

The Configuration Management Database (CMDB) acts as the foundational repository for IT assets and their relationships, powering effective incident, change, and problem management while supporting automation across ITSM processes.

  • Maintain Data Accuracy: Conduct regular audits and updates of Configuration Item (CI) records to ensure they accurately reflect real-world asset relationships and dependencies.
  • Leverage Integrations: Integrate ServiceNow with discovery tools like ServiceNow Discovery to automate data synchronization, keeping the CMDB current without manual intervention.
  • Implement Relationships: Define precise horizontal and vertical relationships between CIs to visualize impact analysis and enable proactive issue resolution during incidents or changes.
  • Adopt ITIL Alignment: Structure the CMDB according to ITIL configuration management practices, using classes like cmdb_ci_server or cmdb_ci_network_gear for standardized data modeling.

This script example demonstrates querying the CMDB to associate an incident with its affected CI:

var incident = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (incident.get(current.getValue('sys_id'))) {
  var cmdbCi = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci');
  cmdbCi.addQuery('name', incident.affected_ci);
  cmdbCi.query();
  if (cmdbCi.next()) {
    incident.cmdb_ci = cmdbCi.sys_id;
    incident.update();
  }
}

An accurate CMDB directly enhances automation by providing reliable data for Flow Designer triggers and actions, such as routing incidents based on CI ownership.

Introduction to Flow Designer for Workflow Automation

Flow Designer is ServiceNow's no-code, drag-and-drop tool for building scalable automations, replacing legacy Workflow Editor with intuitive components like triggers, actions, subflows, and spokes to optimize ITSM workflows efficiently.

Key components include:

  • Triggers: Define when a flow starts, such as record creation on the Incident table with conditions like high priority.
  • Actions: Reusable steps like Create Record, Send Email, or Ask for Approval, sourced from core actions or application-specific spokes like ITSM Spoke.
  • Subflows: Modular, reusable sequences of actions that promote maintainability across multiple parent flows.
  • Data Pills: Drag-and-drop references to action outputs, ensuring flows adapt dynamically without breaking scripts.

Flow Designer supports spokes—scoped applications with pre-built actions for tables like Incident or Problem—activated via plugins or the ServiceNow Store for extended ITSM capabilities.

Optimizing Workflows with Flow Designer Best Practices

Workflow optimization in ServiceNow leverages Flow Designer's modular architecture to create efficient, error-resilient automations tailored for ITSM, from incident routing to change approvals.

  • Migrate from Legacy Workflows: Convert existing workflows to Flow Designer using built-in tools, starting with Utah release features that refactor actions into subflows automatically for better scalability.
  • Use Modular Subflows: Build department-specific subflows, like IT provisioning or HR onboarding, passing record references instead of multiple inputs to reduce complexity and enhance reusability.
  • Implement Error Handlers: Apply flow-level handlers, action-specific conditions, and Try logic to capture diagnostics, notify admins, and allow recovery without halting the entire process.
  • Leverage Decision Tables: Replace complex if-else logic with visual tables for routing approvals or assignments based on CI attributes or incident priority.
  • Automate Incident Routing: Combine machine learning categorization with CMDB relationships to prioritize, assign, and notify based on CI ownership dynamically.
  • Build Incrementally with Testing: Develop flows iteratively, testing success and error paths in a safe environment before production deployment to minimize risks.

Consider this Flow Designer example for high-priority incident email notifications: Trigger on Incident creation where priority is 1 (Critical), then use Send Email action with data pills from the incident record to notify the assignment group.

// Simulated Flow Designer logic in script step
var grInc = new GlideRecord('incident');
grInc.addQuery('priority', 1);
grInc.query();
while (grInc.next()) {
  gs.eventQueue('incident.high.priority', grInc, 'assigned_to', gs.getUserID());
}

For a practical ITSM use case, automate user onboarding via a Service Catalog trigger: Submit catalog item, seek manager approval, create sys_user record, assign to CI groups from CMDB, and update requested-for fields—all orchestrated in one flow with subflows for provisioning.

Integrating CMDB with Flow Designer for ITSM Efficiency

Combining CMDB accuracy with Flow Designer unlocks advanced ITSM automation, such as impact analysis during changes or automated routing using CI dependencies.

Example script within a Flow Designer action to route incidents by CMDB-owned group:

var grInc = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (grInc.get(current.sys_id)) {
  var ci = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci');
  if (ci.get(grInc.cmdb_ci)) {
    grInc.assignment_group = ci.owned_by;
    grInc.update();
  }
}

This integration ensures decisions are data-driven, reducing MTTR (Mean Time to Resolution) by proactively identifying affected services via CMDB relationships.

Conclusion: Achieving ITSM Excellence

By maintaining a precise CMDB and optimizing workflows with Flow Designer, organizations achieve proactive, efficient ITSM operations aligned with ITIL, delivering faster resolutions and superior service quality.

title: Flow Designer Transaction Boundaries: What Every ServiceNow Developer Must Know
excerpt: Flow Designer executes asynchronously with no native rollback. Learn how transactions commit, when to use business rules instead, and proven compensating transaction patterns.
content:
Understanding Flow Designer's Execution Model

Flow Designer typically runs asynchronously relative to the record write that triggered it. That means the triggering database transaction commits first, then the flow runs in a separate execution context. The important implication: there is no single, multi-step database transaction spanning all actions inside a flow.

What This Means in Practice

Each action that writes to the database commits independently. If a later step fails (integration timeout, missing data, unexpected state), earlier updates are already committed.

// Typical flow timeline (conceptual)
// 1) Trigger: Incident created (record commit happens)
// 2) Action: Update CI (commits)
// 3) Action: Create Task (commits)
// 4) Action: REST call fails
// Result: CI update + Task are already in the database

When to Use Business Rules Instead

If you need logic to run inside the same database transaction as the record write, Flow Designer is usually the wrong tool. A Before Business Rule runs before the record is committed, allowing you to validate and set values safely.

ScenarioUse Business RuleUse Flow Designer
Must run before DB write✓ Before BR✗
Same transaction required✓ Before/After BR (carefully)✗
Long-running process✗✓ Async
Multi-step orchestration✗✓
External integrations with retries✗✓

Production Patterns That Work

1) Compensating Transactions

Instead of rollback, you implement a deliberate "undo" step if something fails: close the task you created, revert a field, write an audit note, etc.

2) Idempotency

Design actions so re-running them does not duplicate work. For example, create tasks with a unique key (incident + purpose) and check if it already exists before creating a new one.

3) State Machines Over "Do Everything At Once"

For complex workflows, store a state on the record (or a related orchestration table) and advance it step-by-step. This makes retries safe and failures diagnosable.

Minimal Example: Safe Task Creation

// Prevent duplicate tasks (idempotent create)
var t = new GlideRecord('task');
t.addQuery('parent', current.getUniqueValue());
t.addQuery('short_description', 'Follow-up approval');
t.setLimit(1);
t.query();
if (!t.next()) {
  t.initialize();
  t.parent = current.getUniqueValue();
  t.short_description = 'Follow-up approval';
  t.insert();
}

Conclusion

Flow Designer is excellent for orchestration, but it is not a database transaction manager. Treat every write as "committed forever", design for retries, and use compensating patterns when you need consistency across steps.

title: Scoped Application Security Patterns: Cross-Scope Access Done Right
excerpt: Navigate ServiceNow's scoped application security model with confidence. Learn cross-scope access patterns, ACL evaluation order, and security best practices.
content:
Why Scoped Security Trips Teams Up

In scoped applications, security is not just ACLs. You also have to manage cross-scope behavior: which app can call which APIs, and which app can access which tables. The goal is safe reuse without accidentally granting broad access.

ACL Evaluation Order

ACLs evaluate from most specific to least specific:

  1. Field-level on specific table
  2. Table-level on specific table
  3. Field-level wildcard
  4. Table-level wildcard

GlideRecordSecure vs GlideRecord

// GlideRecordSecure automatically enforces ACLs
var grs = new GlideRecordSecure('incident');
grs.query();
while (grs.next()) {
  // Only returns records user can read
}

// GlideRecord requires manual checks
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  if (gr.canRead()) {
    // Safe to display
  }
}

Cross-Scope Access: Practical Patterns

1) Prefer Application Access on Tables

If a scoped app must read/write another app's table, start with table-level Application Access settings (and keep it as narrow as possible).

2) Use Explicit Cross-Scope Privileges

When a scoped app needs to call an API in another scope, define explicit privileges instead of broad global access. This creates an audit trail and prevents accidental dependency creep.

3) Keep Client-Callable Surface Area Small

Client-callable Script Includes increase your attack surface. Expose only the exact methods needed, validate inputs, and return minimal data.

Security Anti-Patterns to Avoid

  • Using session tricks to bypass ACLs
  • Hardcoding admin credentials in integrations
  • Making all Script Includes client-callable
  • Storing sensitive data in client-accessible fields
  • Using eval() or dynamic script execution

Conclusion

Good scoped security is about intentional boundaries: least-privilege ACLs, explicit cross-scope permissions, and minimal client-callable exposure. If you can explain your access model in one diagram, you're probably doing it right.

title: Predictive Intelligence Deep Dive: Requirements, Limitations, and Production Patterns
excerpt: Predictive Intelligence requires minimum 10,000 records for classification training. Learn the real requirements, common misconceptions, and patterns for production ML implementations.
content:
Predictive Intelligence Components

Predictive Intelligence is a set of ML capabilities that learn from historical data to recommend or predict values on new records.

  • Classification: Auto-categorization / assignment recommendations
  • Similarity: Find related records ("tickets like this")
  • Clustering: Discover hidden groupings / patterns
  • Regression: Predict numeric values

Critical Training Requirements

Classification requires a minimum of 10,000 records for training. In real production implementations, more data typically improves coverage and stability.

Model TypeMinimum RecordsRecommended
Classification10,00050,000+
Similarity1,00010,000+
Clustering5,00025,000+

Data Quality: The Real Make-or-Break

  • Label consistency: assignment group/category values must be stable (avoid frequent renames)
  • Noise reduction: remove misrouted tickets from the training set
  • Class balance: if one group owns 90% of tickets, your model will look "accurate" but be useless

Common Misconception: Major Incident Prediction

Major incident detection commonly uses similarity models to find tickets similar to existing major incidents—it does not magically predict brand new categories of major incidents with no precedent.

Production Patterns

1) Human-in-the-loop rollouts

Start with recommendations (not auto-updates). Let agents accept/reject. Use that feedback to clean labels and retrain.

2) Guardrails

Only apply predictions when confidence is above a threshold, and always log when the system changed a value automatically.

3) Retraining cadence

Plan retraining when org structure changes (new teams, major routing changes) and when ticket distributions drift.

Simple Example: Applying a Predicted Group Safely

// Example: apply predicted group only when present
if (!current.assignment_group.nil() || current.u_predicted_group.nil()) {
  return;
}

current.assignment_group = current.u_predicted_group;
current.work_notes = 'Assignment set by Predictive Intelligence recommendation.';

Conclusion

Predictive Intelligence is strongest when your data is clean and your operating model is stable. Treat it like a product: curate the dataset, roll out gradually, and measure outcomes (MTTR, reassignment rates, and acceptance rate) instead of chasing accuracy alone.

title: Yokohama MFA Enforcement: What You Need to Know Before Upgrading
excerpt: Multi-factor authentication is mandatory in Yokohama with a 90-day grace period. Here's everything you need to configure before upgrading.
content:
Critical Breaking Change

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enabled and required by default for all local login users starting with the Yokohama release. This mandatory enforcement applies to internal users without the snc_external role using local or LDAP authentication, adding an essential security layer to protect your ServiceNow instance.

What is Multi-Factor Authentication?

MFA requires users to provide two or more verification factors to gain access to the instance, such as something they know (password) and something they have (authenticator app code). This significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized access from compromised credentials. ServiceNow supports authenticator apps like Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator that generate time-based one-time passwords (TOTP).

90-Day Grace Period Details

For the first 90 days after upgrading to Yokohama, internal users (without snc_external role) logging in with local or LDAP authentication can access the instance normally but must enroll in MFA within 30 days of their first successful login. Users will see a prominent enrollment prompt during login. After 30 days, MFA becomes mandatory for login. After the full 90 days, MFA enforcement is strict with no self-enrollment grace period for new logins—admins can extend this up to 270 days if needed.

Pre-Upgrade Checklist

  1. Audit current authentication and identify all local login users
  2. Configure MFA policies before upgrade
  3. Test in non-production environments
  4. Communicate to users 2-4 weeks in advance
  5. Prepare support team for MFA-related tickets
  6. Review and set exemptions as needed

title: Upgrade Regression Testing Framework: ATF Patterns for ServiceNow Customizations
excerpt: Build a comprehensive automated testing framework for ServiceNow upgrades. Learn ATF patterns, test suite organization, and CI/CD integration.
content:
Upgrade Regression Testing Framework: ATF Patterns for ServiceNow Customizations

This guide provides a practical automated testing framework for ServiceNow upgrades using the Automated Test Framework (ATF). It covers suite organization, reusable patterns, and how to think about coverage so your customizations survive upgrades without silent regressions.

Why Upgrade Testing Fails and Why ATF Matters

Most upgrade failures occur because customizations like business rules, UI policies, client scripts, ACLs, and integrations break silently after upgrades. ATF solves this by enabling automated, repeatable tests that validate functionality before and after upgrades.

Test Suite Organization

  • Smoke Suite: Validates core platform functionality (5-10 minutes)
  • Regression Suite: Comprehensive coverage of key customizations (30-60 minutes)
  • Integration Suite: Tests external connections and APIs (15-30 minutes)
  • Security Suite: Validates ACL/role behavior and critical access paths
  • UI/Portal Suite: Validates service portals, UI Builder, and custom UIs

Critical ATF Test Patterns

1) Business Rule Validation

// Pattern: Test Business Rule on Incident table
// 1. Impersonate itil user
// 2. Open New Incident form
// 3. Set short_description = 'Test BR Trigger'
// 4. Submit form
// 5. Query Incident by number
// 6. Assert expected fields set by BR

2) Catalog Item Flow Validation

// Pattern: Order a catalog item
// 1. Open Service Catalog item
// 2. Fill variables
// 3. Submit
// 4. Assert RITM created
// 5. Assert flow created tasks/approvals as expected

3) Integration Contract Tests

// Pattern: Validate outbound REST message configuration
// 1. Execute REST message in ATF
// 2. Assert status code is within allowed set (200/201/202)
// 3. Assert response body contains required keys
// 4. Assert error handler path behaves as expected

CI/CD Integration (High-Level)

A common production pattern is to run Smoke + targeted Regression suites on every deployment to a sub-prod environment, then run the full Regression suite during upgrade testing windows. Keep test data stable and minimize dependencies on volatile records.

Best Practices

  • Name tests by business outcome, not implementation detail
  • Make tests deterministic (avoid "today" where possible)
  • Prefer smaller tests that fail fast
  • Maintain tests alongside code (same app/version control)
  • Routinely prune obsolete tests after refactors

Conclusion

ATF is your upgrade insurance. The most effective framework is one you can run frequently, interpret quickly, and trust. Start small (smoke suite), then expand coverage around the processes your business cannot afford to break.

title: Now Assist Consumption Optimization: Managing Your 'Assists' Budget
excerpt: Now Assist uses a consumption-based 'assists' model with Pro Plus licensing. Learn strategies to optimize usage and maximize ROI.
content:
Understanding Now Assist Licensing

Now Assist is commonly sold as an add-on aligned to higher-tier licensing (for example, Pro Plus / Enterprise Plus depending on the product area). The practical impact: you should treat generative AI usage like a budgeted resource and measure it like you would a cloud bill.

What Counts as an Assist?

  • Incident/case summarization
  • Knowledge article suggestions
  • Resolution recommendations
  • Email draft generation
  • Code suggestions in Studio
  • Virtual Agent AI responses

Optimization Strategies

1) Target High-Value Use Cases

  • Complex incidents with long resolution times
  • Customer-facing communications
  • Knowledge creation from resolved tickets
  • Code reviews in development

2) Implement Usage Guardrails

Common guardrails include per-user daily limits, role-based enablement, and restricting certain assist types to specific groups (e.g., L2/L3 only).

var UserAssistLimit = Class.create();
UserAssistLimit.prototype = {
  initialize: function(userId) {
    this.userId = userId;
    this.dailyLimit = parseInt(gs.getProperty('now_assist.daily_limit', '50'), 10);
  },

  canUseAssist: function() {
    // Placeholder: check today's usage count for this.userId
    // Return true if usage < this.dailyLimit
    return true;
  },

  type: 'UserAssistLimit'
};

3) Reduce Low-Value Calls

  • Don’t summarize tiny incidents (use minimum length thresholds)
  • Don’t draft emails that are auto-responses anyway
  • Cache summaries for unchanged records

Measure ROI

Track assists used vs outcomes: MTTR reduction, fewer reassignments, higher first-contact resolution, and knowledge deflection. Without outcome metrics, consumption optimization becomes guesswork.

Conclusion

Now Assist works best when you treat it like a product: pick the highest-value journeys, enforce guardrails, and measure outcomes. Done right, you get the speed of GenAI without surprise bills or messy governance.
